headline: PLS tanks 6% on results day while the RBA hints at more rate hikes — a mixed Tuesday on the Gold Coast.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS had a tough session today despite posting a 152% surge in FY26 revenue as the lithium market recovers. The market seems to be selling the news — investors are worried about whether the expansion plans at Pilgangoora will deliver, and near-term lithium price uncertainty is keeping a lid on enthusiasm. Big day-move, but the longer-term recovery story is still intact.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped last night as a wave of GTA 6 gameplay leaks — now six straight days of them — rattled some investor confidence. A former Rockstar director called the leaks a 'nothing burger', but the market is nervous about IP security and launch momentum heading into what should be the biggest game release in years.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: A minor dip today in the ASX session. No specific news catalyst — the broader AI sector ETF just gave back a small amount after recent gains. The NASDAQ was softer last night which may have weighed on sentiment heading into today's open.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft nudged higher last night, continuing to ride the AI wave. No major news catalyst, but the stock remains well-supported as investors back its Azure cloud and Copilot AI products as long-term winners.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Alphabet gained last night off the back of strong Q2 2026 AI and cloud momentum — the market is rewarding Google's progress in catching up in the AI race. Earnings are also on the radar with Zacks flagging it as a key upcoming preview.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: A quiet positive session today. Emerging markets got a small lift — likely helped by a slightly weaker USD and ongoing China stimulus hopes. Nothing dramatic, just steady.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: Edged up today on the ASX, tracking last night's mixed US session. The S&P and NASDAQ were both slightly down last night, but VTS still managed a small gain — likely a mild AUD tailwind effect as the Aussie dollar softened slightly.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: A gentle positive session — VDHG's diversified mix of global shares did its job, absorbing some volatility and ticking modestly higher. Nothing to worry about here; it's doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Big drop today — but hold your nerve
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals fell 6% today despite reporting FY26 revenue up 152% as lithium markets recover. This looks like classic 'sell the news' behaviour. The long-term thesis — a lithium price recovery and Pilgangoora expansion — hasn't changed. You're already sitting at a 23.7% loss, so selling now locks that in. Hold and let the lithium story play out.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA 6 leak drama — stay the course
watch_today.detail: Take-Two dropped 2.55% last night after six consecutive days of GTA 6 gameplay leaks. A former Rockstar director called it a 'nothing burger' and the core long-term thesis — that GTA 6 will be one of the biggest-selling games ever — is unchanged. Your position is barely above water (+0.57%), so this is a hold and watch situation, not a reason to bail.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: Small dip, long-term story intact
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF slipped a fraction today (-0.43%) — no specific news, just a quiet session. It's your biggest loss position (-14.97%), which stings, but the AI sector growth story is a genuine long-term megatrend. Holding makes sense for a buy-and-hold investor. Only consider topping up if you have spare cash and conviction — this dip alone isn't a strong signal either way.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike risk is back on the table
watch_today.detail: Today's RBA minutes revealed the board was genuinely divided at the August meeting — several members were pushing for another rate hike. The AFR is reporting 'several board members eye another rate rise.' Higher rates generally drag on growth stocks and put upward pressure on the AUD, which can reduce the AUD value of your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO). Keep an eye on the next RBA meeting.

watch_today.title: MSFT & GOOG: Both up last night — US tech holding firm
watch_today.detail: Both Microsoft (+0.84%) and Alphabet (+0.83%) gained last night. Google is being rewarded for strong Q2 AI and cloud numbers, and Microsoft continues to benefit from AI tailwinds. Both are solid long-term holds — nothing to do here except sit tight and let compounding do its thing.

watch_today.title: Gold at record highs — a signal of global anxiety
watch_today.detail: Gold hit $4,696 USD per ounce last night, up 1.21%. That's a massive number. Gold tends to spike when investors are nervous about geopolitics or economic stability — and right now there's plenty of both (Iran war, US election uncertainty, energy shocks). Your portfolio doesn't hold gold directly, but this is a useful signal that global risk appetite is cautious.

world.summary: A busy day globally — the US-Iran conflict is squeezing American farmers and energy markets, the US Supreme Court has handed Trump a major win on mail-in voting restrictions, and global economic growth is being tested by energy and trade shocks.

stories.title: US Supreme Court clears Trump's mail-in voting crackdown ahead of midterms
stories.why_it_matters: The US Supreme Court has allowed Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting to go ahead, just ahead of the midterm elections. The order limits who can use mail-in ballots and how they're processed — critics say it will disenfranchise millions of voters. The New York Times reports Trump has also been quietly seeking greater control over the US Postal Service to reshape how elections are run. This is a major shift in American democracy that experts say could set a precedent for how future elections are administered.

stories.title: US-Iran war is pushing American grain farmers to the brink
stories.why_it_matters: The Financial Times reports US grain farmers are facing their worst financial crisis in decades, driven by surging fuel and fertiliser costs linked to the ongoing US-Iran conflict. The war has sent energy prices spiralling, with knock-on effects across the entire agricultural supply chain. Higher food production costs in the US typically flow through to global food prices — something that affects every household's grocery bill, including here in Australia.

stories.title: US announces new Iran sanctions, says war entering 'endgame'
stories.why_it_matters: The US government is rolling out a fresh round of sanctions against Iran and is signalling the conflict may be entering its final phase. An Iranian official has responded by warning that international support for the sanctions would be treated as 'an act of war' — escalatory language that suggests tensions remain extremely high. Oil prices are sitting at $84.40/barrel — the ongoing conflict is a key reason energy remains elevated globally.

stories.title: Iran discovers major new gas reserves amid war-ravaged energy sector
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has announced the discovery of significant new natural gas reserves despite the economic damage caused by the war. This is a strategic long-term play — if Iran can eventually bring those reserves to market, it could significantly affect global gas supply and pricing. For now it's a future signal, but worth watching given how much energy markets are already in flux.

stories.title: Global Q3 2026 economic outlook: growth under pressure from energy and trade shocks
stories.why_it_matters: Euromonitor's Q3 2026 global economic outlook warns that growth is being tested by simultaneous energy and trade shocks — largely stemming from the Iran conflict and its ripple effects. This matters for your portfolio: a slowing global economy typically drags on corporate earnings, which flows through to share prices. It's a useful backdrop for understanding why markets have been choppy.

markets.summary: The ASX had a solid session today, up 0.68% to 9,164. Last night in the US it was a different story — the S&P 500 dipped 0.28% and the NASDAQ fell 0.76%, as tech took a breather. Gold surged to near-record territory at $4,697, oil slipped slightly, and the Aussie dollar eased a touch against the USD.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today — Australian shares pushed higher, likely helped by commodity strength and positive carry-over from earlier in the week.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw a minor pullback — nothing alarming, just some profit-taking after a strong run.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech was the soft spot last night, with the NASDAQ dropping 0.76%. Growth stocks came under mild pressure, though MSFT and GOOG bucked the trend.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Gold is flying — up over 1.2% last night to near $4,700/oz. Investors are piling into safe havens amid geopolitical tension and US political uncertainty.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil eased slightly last night despite ongoing Middle East conflict. Still elevated by historical standards.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar dipped slightly — down about a third of a cent. A softer AUD means your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) are worth slightly more in AUD terms.

politics.summary: Big RBA news today — the minutes from the August meeting reveal real division on the board about another rate hike. Plus the federal government is pushing new data centre rules that Queensland is pushing back on, and the ACT is introducing a gun buyback scheme backed by Albanese.

stories.title: RBA was split on rate hike in August — and another rise is still on the table
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA's August meeting minutes, released today, show the board was genuinely divided about whether to raise interest rates again. Several members backed another hike, while others wanted to hold. The RBA says higher rates are still working to bring down inflation, but risks remain. CommBank noted that while the board is reluctant to hike, they haven't ruled it out — meaning Australian mortgage holders and businesses aren't in the clear yet. Watch for the next meeting decision carefully.

stories.title: Federal government pushes new data centre rules — Queensland pushes back
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is pushing new national rules around data centres — covering things like energy use, location, and security standards. Queensland has come out against the federal proposals, flagging concerns about state sovereignty and the impact on local infrastructure investment. As AI and cloud computing drive massive growth in data centre construction globally, who controls the rules around them is increasingly a big economic and political battleground.

stories.title: ACT introduces gun buyback — Albanese government backs expanded firearms reforms
stories.why_it_matters: The ACT is rolling out a gun buyback program, with the federal government backing a broader expansion of firearms reforms nationally. The Albanese government's support signals this could become a wider policy push. Gun reform is politically sensitive in Australia — the 1996 Port Arthur buyback is still seen as one of the most successful policy interventions in the nation's history, so any new iteration will be watched closely.

stories.title: RBA appoints Melinda Cilento to interest rate board
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA has announced that Melinda Cilento — an economist and former CEDA chief — will join the interest rate board. Board composition matters: new members bring different economic philosophies, and given the board is already divided on whether to hike rates again, Cilento's appointment could shift the balance of future decisions. Something to watch as the rate debate continues.

ai.summary: Today's AI news is dominated by regulation debates — how should governments control AI before it causes harm? Meanwhile, Thomson Reuters has launched its own in-house AI legal model, and a new coding AI called Ox Alpha has emerged.

stories.title: Tyler Cowen: The least bad way to regulate AI
stories.why_it_matters: Economist Tyler Cowen has published a widely-read piece arguing that most AI regulation proposals are flawed — either too slow to matter or too blunt to be useful. His core argument is that governments should focus on being flexible and outcome-based rather than trying to regulate specific AI models. This is a mainstream debate now, not a fringe one — the rules governments set in the next few years will shape which companies (and countries) win the AI race.

stories.title: Thomson Reuters launches its own AI model for legal document reviews
stories.why_it_matters: Thomson Reuters — the global legal and news data giant — has launched its own proprietary AI model specifically designed to review legal documents. This is significant: rather than using off-the-shelf tools like ChatGPT, they've built a bespoke model trained on their vast legal databases. It's a signal that large enterprises are moving beyond generic AI and building specialised tools — which is the next phase of AI adoption that companies like Google (your GOOG holding) and Microsoft (MSFT) are betting on.

stories.title: Ox Alpha emerges as a powerful new AI coding model
stories.why_it_matters: A new AI model called Ox Alpha has surfaced, positioning itself as a strong competitor in the AI coding space — the increasingly crowded market of tools that write, review, and fix software code. Competition in AI coding tools is fierce, with Google's Gemini, Microsoft's GitHub Copilot, and Anthropic's Claude all fighting for dominance. More competition is ultimately good for developers but puts pressure on incumbents to keep innovating — relevant for your GOOG and MSFT holdings.

stories.title: Australia criticised for lacking AI strategy as 'conundrum' deepens
stories.why_it_matters: The Nightly is running a piece arguing Prime Minister Albanese is not up to the challenge of developing a coherent national AI strategy. As other nations race to set rules and invest in AI infrastructure, Australia risks being left behind without a clear framework. For investors in AI-exposed assets (like your GXAI.AX ETF), Australia's regulatory direction matters — it affects which local companies can operate, attract talent, and compete globally.

sport.summary: NRL Round 26 draws are set for the weekend with the Broncos hosting Storm on Thursday night at Suncorp. Meanwhile a huge NRL signing has been unveiled, there's big AFL finals news, and a Sydney Swans controversy is making headlines.

stories.title: Tigers pull off 'upset of the year' — stunning first-place Roosters
stories.why_it_matters: The Wests Tigers pulled off what Fox Sports is calling the 'upset of the year', knocking off the first-place Sydney Roosters. A big blow for the Roosters with finals positioning on the line, and a massive confidence booster for the Tigers who have been battling all season. Fox Sports also flagged a verdict on a Roosters star following the match — worth checking for injury or judiciary news ahead of Round 26.

stories.title: PNG Chiefs unveil Joey Manu as stunning '007' signing
stories.why_it_matters: The PNG Chiefs have landed a massive signing, luring former Roosters and New Zealand representative Joey Manu back to the NRL. Manu is one of the most electric backs in the game and his signing as the 'agent 007' mystery player had fans guessing for days. This is a huge statement from the PNG Chiefs as they build their identity in the competition.

stories.title: AFL finals: Wildcard games and full Week 2 schedule locked in
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL has confirmed the full finals schedule including Wildcard weekend and Week 2 fixtures. With finals now underway, the fixture is set — teams know when and where they play. If you're following any clubs in contention, now's the time to lock in your plans.

stories.title: Swans cocaine allegations — dad of player furious at claims
stories.why_it_matters: A Sydney Swans player's father has publicly and angrily denied cocaine use allegations against his son, with the story becoming a significant off-field distraction for the club right in the middle of AFL finals. No player has been named officially, but the story is gaining momentum. Controversial off-field news during finals is the last thing any club wants.
